Optimization/prediction method used: Continuous approximation (analytical synchronization of travel times) sets the zone of each mode and the drone speed; an ILP for the discrete case is stated for small instances but not run in the simulation; simulation-based scenario comparison
Comments: A last-mile delivery concept is simulated in which a delivery van parks on the main street of a stylized fishbone neighborhood and dispatches a driver, street robots and drones to deliver heavy and light parcels along the side-streets. A discrete-event model in Plant Simulation applies a synchronization rule that assigns houses to modes and fixes the drone speed so that all modes return together. Compared with the driver delivering alone, drones and street robots cut the makespan sharply when few parcels are heavy, the driver only helps when heavy parcels or density grow, and the fleet mix with the lowest makespan also gives low drone energy use.
Any attributes: Main street (length 1000 m), side-streets (20, length uniform with low, medium or high variability), houses (spacing 10 m, share visited set by delivery density 10, 20 or 40%), parcels (heavy or light, heavy share 5, 10 or 20%), delivery van (one; speed 15 km/h; capacity of drones d and street robots s), truck driver (walking speed 4 km/h, one parcel at a time), street robots (speed 5 km/h, one parcel, accessibility share), drones (speed set by synchronization, one parcel, accessibility share, safe flying height), on-site delivery time, delivery scenario (driver alone, driver and drones, robots and drones, driver, robots and drones), fleet composition (decision variable); performance: Makespan (total completion time), working time per delivery mode, drone energy consumption

Title: Simulating Truck Fleet Configuration for Wood Terminals
Specific aspect / SC aspect: Analysis and optimization: numbers of self-loading trucks, prime mover trucks and semitrailers that minimize cost per ton and maximize weekly turnover in a multi-echelon unimodal wood SC (forest landings, transshipment terminals, industry), over transport distance, terminal utilization, truck payload and number of transshipment lots
Optimization/prediction method used: Full enumeration of fleet configurations by simulation runs, compared with heuristic solutions
Comments: A two-page summary of a discrete event model of wood transport from forest landings by self-loading trucks to transshipment terminals and on to industry by semitrailer trucks, built to relieve the shortage of self-loading truck capacity after forest calamities. Fleet configurations are enumerated for terminals with 2, 4, 6 and 8 transshipment lots under different distances, terminal utilizations and payloads. Optimal fleets beat unimodal transport cost benchmarks by 5.45%, 6.95% and 11.28% for short, medium and long distances, terminal size cuts cost per ton, and higher payloads reduce the trucks needed.
Any attributes: Forest landings, transshipment terminal (2, 4, 6 or 8 transshipment lots), industry, self-loading trucks, semitrailers and prime mover trucks (numbers are decisions, 3 to 51, 8 to 70 and 7 to 65 in the optimal fleets), truck payload, transport distance (short, medium, long), terminal utilization, process times, operating costs, weekly turnover; performance: Cost per ton, turnover in tons per week, queuing, working and transport times, utilization of each truck type, saved working time, saved number of self-loading trucks

Title: Simulation-Based Aircraft Spare Parts Optimization with Operational Objectives and Constraints
Specific aspect / SC aspect: Analysis and optimization: reorder points of about 35,000 spare parts at the 40+ stations of an airline, set by hill climbing on simulated aircraft-out-of-service events, either at the current inventory investment or to meet a daily target
Optimization/prediction method used: Hill climbing on station reorder points, raising the reorder point of the station with the most simulated aircraft-out-of-service events until the target is met
Comments: A two-page industrial case of a simulation-based optimization deployed at a major international carrier. The simulation follows the flight schedule, part usage, scheduled and unscheduled maintenance, purchase orders, repair cycles, expedited deliveries and borrowing between stations, and reports service level and aircraft-out-of-service events per station and for the network. Hill climbing then raises station reorder points until a target is met. Rebalancing the current inventory cut simulated aircraft-out-of-service events by 25%, and a daily target cut them by 35% with about 12% less inventory value.
Any attributes: Aircraft (700+), flight schedule (5000+ flights per day), stations (40+), parts (about 35,000), part usage events, scheduled and unscheduled maintenance, aircraft overnight rests, part criticality, purchase orders, repair cycles, expedited deliveries, borrowing between stations, reorder point per part and station (decision, initial value zero), inventory value; performance: Aircraft-out-of-service events (monthly average, per station and network), service level, delays and cancellations, inventory value

Title: Supply Chain Reduction in Regulated Markets
Specific aspect / SC aspect: Analysis: effect on total SC cost and end-to-end lead time of removing one echelon from an antibody manufacturing and distribution chain (as-is chain of raw supplier, tier 1 plant and DC, OEM plant and DC, customer against a chain without the tier 1 stage)
Optimization/prediction method used: Simulation-based scenario comparison of the as-is and the complexity-reduced chain, with a sensitivity analysis
Comments: A two-page industrial case of a life-science company's antibody supply chain, modeled in Arena with one year of data from a global supply network. The as-is chain runs from a raw material supplier through a tier 1 plant and distribution center and an OEM plant and distribution center to the customer, with reorder-point policies at the buffers. The redesigned chain drops the tier 1 stage and keeps two manufacturing steps at the OEM. The redesign cut total SC cost by 38.2% (processing cost 54.6%, inventory holding cost 26.7%) and end-to-end lead time by 9.4%, and a sensitivity analysis found the result robust.
Any attributes: Raw material supplier (tier 2), tier 1 plant and distribution center, OEM plant and distribution center, customer, raw material and finished goods buffers, manufacturing steps (one or two at the OEM), reorder point and order quantity at each buffer, transit and lead times, processing times, processing, logistics and transportation and inventory holding costs, as-is and complexity-reduced designs (decision), one year of demand data; performance: Total SC cost (processing, logistics and transportation, inventory holding), processing time, logistics and transportation time, end-to-end lead time

Title: A Simulation-Heuristic Approach to Optimally Design Drone Delivery Systems in Rural Areas
Specific aspect / SC aspect: Analysis and optimization: placement of drone depots and charging stations among candidate sites in Knox County, Tennessee, to serve 80 to 101 customers at minimum setup and penalty cost, found by a genetic algorithm that evaluates each design in an agent-based model, with sensitivity analyses on drone flight range and on the depot to charging station cost ratio
Optimization/prediction method used: Genetic algorithm inside the simulation (simheuristic), compared with a greedy heuristic; an integer program solved with Gurobi for small instances only
Comments: Drone delivery to rural customers is limited by flight range, so charging stations extend the range of a few costly depots. The siting problem is written as an integer program, which Gurobi cannot solve at 50 customers, 3 depots and 40 stations. An AnyLogic agent-based model on a GIS map therefore checks, for any candidate design, which customers a drone can reach from a depot through chained charging stations and adds a penalty for the rest, and a genetic algorithm searches the designs. On 101 customers, 4 candidate depots and 67 candidate stations the genetic algorithm needs one depot and one station and costs 17 to 30% less than a greedy heuristic, and flight range below 6 km breaks the design.
Any attributes: Customers (80 or 101, GIS locations from census data), candidate drone depots (4, at UPS store locations, setup cost 1 million USD), candidate charging stations (55 or 67, setup cost 10,000 USD), siting of depots and stations (decision), drone flight range (uniform 4 to 8 km, 6 to 9 km, or fixed 5, 6, 7.5, 9 km), penalty for an unserved customer (100,000 USD), depot to charging station cost ratio (10:1 to 1:1); performance: Total cost (setup and penalty), number of customers served, number of depots and stations placed

Title: Closing the Gap: A Digital Twin as a Mechanism to Improve Spare Parts Planning Performance
Specific aspect / SC aspect: Analysis: gap between the expected performance of optimized base stock levels in ASML's multi-echelon spare parts network and the performance of a digital twin, split into causes (human review of stock levels, network and process complexity, demand and lead time uncertainty) by switching each cause on or off
Optimization/prediction method used: Simulation-based scenario comparison with on-off switches for each cause of the gap
Comments: A semiconductor equipment maker sets base stock levels for spare parts with a planning model that assumes an infinite horizon, Poisson demand and an unlimited global stock. A discrete-event digital twin of the service network, with local and global warehouses, lateral transshipments between warehouses in a region and emergency shipments, reproduces the planning model when all switches are off and is checked against it. Switching causes on one by one shows that realized demand and the other factors lower the direct fill rate and raise holding costs for most local warehouses, while realized performance in practice is higher than the twin's.
Any attributes: Global warehouses (2), local warehouses (8 in the test set, grouped into regions), factories as an unlimited emergency source, plan groups (machines at customer sites with an SLA), SKUs, base stock level per SKU and warehouse (input), demand (Poisson per plan group and SKU, or actual history), supplier lead time and replenishment lead time (6 to 29 days), transportation time (Gamma distributed), repair flow and return of unused parts, replenishment rule (FIFO or non-availability risk), starting stock, holding, lateral transshipment and emergency transport costs, the twelve on-off switches (review by tactical planners, review by field planners, engineer behavior, global warehouse coupling, demand fulfillment, replenishment logic, return of unused parts, return of repaired parts, actual demand, current stock, stochastic transport times, stochastic supplier lead times); performance: Direct, local and regional fill rate, lateral transshipment rate, emergency shipment rate, holding cost, transport cost, inventory turnover

Title: Improvement of the Kanban System for an Automotive Company via Discrete Event Simulation: Otokar
Specific aspect / SC aspect: Optimization: kanban bin sizes, warehouse critical and maximum stock levels (s, S) and the mizusumashi review period for three supplied parts of one vehicle assembly line, to minimize work in process without stockouts
Optimization/prediction method used: OptQuest search over kanban size, s, S and review period, minimizing work in process subject to no stockouts
Comments: A two-page extended abstract on the kanban supply of an automotive manufacturer's assembly line. Three parts with different usage and lead times are drawn from a two-bin kanban system refilled by a mizusumashi, and a warehouse is replenished from a supplier by an (s, S) rule with a lead time. The model is built in Arena and the control variables are searched with OptQuest. No result is reported.
Any attributes: Parts per vehicle, vehicle arrival, assembly time, kanban bins and kanban size, mizusumashi review period, warehouse stock, critical stock level (s), maximum stock level (S), supplier lead time; performance: work in process, stockouts

Title: Quality Driven Transport Strategies for the Wood Supply Chain
Specific aspect / SC aspect: Analysis: the relationship between procurement lead time and the quality devaluation of sawlogs stored at the roadside, used to evaluate transport strategies that prioritize piles at risk
Optimization/prediction method used: Quadratic and cubic regression of downgraded wood volume on lead time; simulation-based scenario comparison of transport strategies
Comments: A two-page extended abstract on a discrete-event model of a wood supply chain in which sawlogs lose quality at the roadside through blue stain and insect infestation. Wood flows from three altitude-zone sources by truck, or by truck and rail via a terminal, to the industry, and transport strategies prioritize the piles at risk using weather-based forecasts. Regressions show that procurement lead time explains over 98 percent of the variance of the downgraded wood volume.
Any attributes: Wood entities (1 cubic meter), piles (25 cubic meter truckloads), harvesting weeks and quantities, three altitude-zone sources, quality deterioration risk forecasts (blue stain, insects), self-loading trucks, rail wagons, terminal, unimodal or multimodal transport, pickup prioritization strategy, daily working times; performance: downgraded wood volume, procurement lead time

Title: Solving Facility Location Problems for Disaster Response Using Simheuristics and Survival Analysis: A Hybrid Modeling Approach
Specific aspect / SC aspect: Analysis and optimization: the locations of a budget-limited number of disaster response facilities that minimize the expected worst travel time to all demand points when road delays are stochastic, with the probability of meeting a target response time estimated by survival analysis
Optimization/prediction method used: Simheuristic: a multi-start biased-randomized savings heuristic that evaluates solutions by Monte Carlo simulation of lognormal travel delays; Kaplan-Meier survival analysis for the risk of missing a target time
Comments: A stochastic facility location model for disaster response in which each facility serves the demand points nearest to it and travel times carry a lognormal delay for road damage. A multi-start heuristic generates solutions and Monte Carlo replications estimate the expected worst makespan, tested on adapted p-median benchmark instances of 500 to 3,000 points. The simheuristic solutions beat the deterministic ones by about 8.9 percent, and a budget analysis and a Kaplan-Meier risk analysis follow.
Any attributes: Demand points, candidate facilities (each point is also a candidate), number of facilities to open (budget), opening cost scheme, deterministic travel time, stochastic travel delay (lognormal, mean ratio r, variance factor c), allocation of points to facilities; performance: expected worst makespan, gap to the deterministic solution, probability of covering all demand points within a target time

Title: A Hybrid Simulation-based Optimization Framework for Managing Modular Bridge Construction Projects: A Cable-Stayed Bridge Case Study

Optimization/prediction method used: OptQuest search for each of fourteen objectives, with the solutions compared by a normalized performance score
Comments: A hybrid model of the supply chain of a modular cable-stayed bridge in Giza, Egypt: steel girders are made in a factory, assembled into modules in a yard, and carried by barge to the bridge, while precast slabs come by truck. Trucks, the barge and traffic are agents, and the factory, yard and onsite works are discrete event processes. A sensitivity analysis picks seven decision variables, and OptQuest finds fourteen solutions that are compared on duration, cost and emissions.

Title: CROSSStacks: A Dataset and a Simulative Study of Storage Allocation Strategies for Cross-Docking Block-Stacking Warehouses
Specific aspect / SC aspect: Optimization: the storage location assignment of pallets in a cross-docking block-stacking terminal served by autonomous mobile robots, comparing five assignment strategies on service time and travel distance, with the number of robots found by a bottleneck analysis
Optimization/prediction method used: Simulation-based scenario comparison of storage location assignment heuristics (Shortest Leg, Closest to the Next Retrieval Order, Closest Open Location, Closest to Destination, random)
Comments: An extension of the open-source SLAPStack simulation framework to cross-docking, with a dataset (CROSSStacks) built from two weeks of orders and the layout of a freight company's cross-docking terminal for food goods. Robots move pallets between 19 inbound and 21 outbound docks and 2,150 storage locations on the ground. Two dual command cycle strategies are compared with three baselines, and Shortest Leg cuts the average service time by about 19 percent against the common destination-based strategy.
Any attributes: Warehouse layout (2,150 storage locations in bays and lanes, 19 inbound and 21 outbound docks), delivery and retrieval orders (SKU, dock, arrival time, destination dock), autonomous mobile robots (number, speed 1.2 m/s), material handling time (45 s), pallet shift penalty (90 s), storage location assignment strategy (decision); performance: average service time, total distance per robot, maximum delivery and retrieval queue length, robot utilization

Title: Integrated Modeling and Optimization of Spare Part Logistic Operations and Condition-based Maintenance Policies in a System of Geographically Distributed Assets
Specific aspect / SC aspect: Analysis and optimization: the location of spare parts logistics centers, the network connectivity, the inventory levels that trigger replenishment and the condition-based maintenance policies of geographically distributed assets with several degrading parts, to minimize the overall operating cost
Optimization/prediction method used: Two stages: a mixed-integer nonlinear program for the logistics network (after Jeet and Kutanoglu 2018), then a metaheuristic over the simulation for maintenance policies and inventory levels
Comments: A two-page poster on a sequential model for spare parts logistics and condition-based maintenance. A mixed-integer nonlinear program first designs the network of spare parts centers, and a discrete event simulation with a continuous time Markov chain for part degradation then gives the maintenance policies and the replenishment levels by a metaheuristic. The results show that a longer spare part lead time makes earlier replacement cheaper and that opportunistic maintenance saves more as the lead time grows.
Any attributes: Spare parts logistics centers (facility location, network connectivity), assets with several degrading parts, degradation states (continuous time Markov chain), preventive replacement condition, replenishment-triggering inventory level, spare part lead time, opportunistic maintenance; performance: overall operating cost of the logistics network and maintenance, unscheduled downtime

Title: Large Scale Logistics Network Simulation and Its Application in JD Logistics
Specific aspect / SC aspect: Analysis and optimization: the number of persons and vehicles, the transportation routes, the stowage of routes and the use of spare sorting hubs in JD Logistics' parcel network during the November 11 promotion, to cut transit time, shipping distance and undeliverable packages
Optimization/prediction method used: Iterative simulation-based improvement with a human in the loop (eight iterations) against the exponential smoothing forecast arrangement
Comments: A discrete event simulator at package level for the parcel network of JD Logistics, with nearly 1,000 sorting hubs and more than 6,000 transportation routes, written as a new engine in Java. Packages are created, carried by road, rail or air, unloaded, sorted and loaded again under hub shifts and gate limits. Eight iterations of simulation and manual adjustment of persons, vehicles and routes for the 2022 promotion lower the transit time by 7 to 19 percent, the shipping distance by 8 percent and the undeliverable packages by 70 percent against the forecast-based arrangement.
Any attributes: Sorting hubs (hourly sorting capacity, shifts, loading and unloading gates by type, location, average package volume and weight), transportation routes (origin, destination, departure and arrival times, road, rail or air, trunk, branch or ferry, vehicle length, stowage hubs), package transport demand (origin, destination, creation time, number), average loading, unloading and sorting times, persons and vehicles; performance: transit time by distance class, shipping distance, sorting times, undeliverable packages

Title: Simulation-based Cost Modeling to Measure the Effect of Automated Trucks in Inter-terminal Container Transportation
Specific aspect / SC aspect: Analysis: the effect of automation, number of vehicles, number of terminals, order volume and road use on the cost per transport of container movements between the terminals of the port of Hamburg, with automated and manual trucks
Optimization/prediction method used: 2^5 factorial design of 32 design points, 50 runs each, feeding a 15-year total cost model
Comments: A discrete event model of container transport between terminals of the port of Hamburg, in which trucks receive orders by a priority rule on urgency and travel time. The simulated orders, mileage and vehicle numbers feed a cost model of purchase and operating costs over 15 years. A two-level factorial design over terminals (4 or 30), orders per terminal (100 or 300), vehicles, automation and exclusive roads shows that automation lowers the cost per transport by about 65 euros, from 87 to 22 euros on average, while the other factors matter little.

Title: Using Simulation to Assess the Reliability of Forecasts in High-tech Industry
Specific aspect / SC aspect: Analysis and prediction: a reliability score for the rolling-horizon demand forecasts that an aerospace parts supplier receives from its customers, an alternative forecast from billed turnover, and their effect on the supplier's production cost in a simulated plant
Optimization/prediction method used: Double exponential smoothing for the reliability score; ARIMA, Prophet, support vector regression and LSTM for the alternative forecast
Comments: A supplier of aerospace parts receives monthly rolling forecasts from its customers and doubts their stability. The paper scores the reliability of each lag period of a forecast with double exponential smoothing and forecasts orders from billed turnover with support vector regression, and tests both in a discrete event model of the supplier's plant. Across 27 scenarios of three customers with low, medium or high forecast reliability, the two methods lower the average plant cost by 14 percent against using the original forecast.
Any attributes: Customer forecasts (rolling horizon, monthly lag periods up to 18), actual orders (billed turnover), customer forecast reliability (low, medium, high) for three customers of low, medium and high volume, product family architecture, production lead time and due date, workforce and machine allocation from the forecast quantity, inventory holding, labor, operating and back-order costs, input scenario (original forecast, most reliable lag period, SVR forecast); performance: total cost, gap to the original-forecast scenario

Title: Relocation of the distribution center of a motor oil producer reducing its storage capacity: A case study
Venue: Simulation: Transactions of the Society for Modeling and Simulation International (SIMULATION)
Specific aspect / SC aspect: Analysis: feasibility of relocating a motor oil producer's distribution center to a smaller automated site beside the plant, in terms of delivery time to distributors, orders shipped, storage use, and dock and parking use under four disruption scenarios
Optimization/prediction method used: Simulation-based scenario comparison, with hypothesis tests on delivery time, service level and capacity
Comments: A ProModel discrete-event model of the supply network of a Mexican motor oil producer: raw-material trailers entering the plant, finished product shipped to a distribution center, and orders sent to 14 distributors. It compares the current distribution center with a smaller automated one beside the plant under four disruption scenarios (a day without deliveries, loading dock stops, closing of sales, unloading dock stops). The relocation lengthens delivery times by about 69 to 107 minutes, but the new center handles the demand with enough docks and parking, so the relocation is judged feasible.
Any attributes: distribution center (relocation, decision; storage locations 17,800 against 10,800), plant output rate (38,250 liters per hour), loading and unloading docks (20 against 3 loading and 1 unloading; five unloading docks and polyethylene and paperboard docks), parking lots (8 and 10 trailers), trailer fleet (20), distributors (14), customer orders (fitted distribution per customer), arrivals of raw material, polyethylene and paperboard trailers, loading, unloading, sampling, weighing and quality-test times, travel time to each distributor (uniform), working schedule and traffic restriction hours, disruption scenarios (a day without deliveries, dock stop of 12 hours twice a year and of a full day, closing of sales with 140 orders, unloading dock stop of two days); performance: delivery time, orders shipped (customer service index), storage utilization of the distribution center, dock and parking utilization, trailers waiting

Title: Coordinating of multi-echelon supply chains through the generalized (R, S) policy
Venue: Simulation: Transactions of the Society for Modeling and Simulation International (SIMULATION)
Specific aspect / SC aspect: Analysis: effect of a coordination mechanism that combines information sharing and order smoothing under the generalized (R, S) policy, together with lead time, smoothing and forecast parameters, on the bullwhip effect and the net stock variance in a six-stage serial chain
Optimization/prediction method used: Simulation-based scenario comparison: full factorial design (16 design points) with ANOVA in Minitab
Comments: A SIMUL8 discrete-event model of a six-stage serial chain with the beer game structure (customer, retailer, wholesaler, distributor, factory, supplier). Each stage orders with a generalized (R, S) order-up-to policy. The proposed Info-Smooth rule passes the demand forecast and the inventory adjustment upstream as two parts of each order. A full factorial experiment varies the collaboration model, lead time, smoothing parameter and forecast length. Info-Smooth lowers both the order variance ratio and the net stock variance ratio compared with the traditional chain, and it is less sensitive to lead time.
Any attributes: serial chain of six nodes (customer, retailer, wholesaler, distributor, factory, supplier), customer demand (normal, mean 30, SD 3), generalized (R, S) order-up-to policy (review period 1, smoothing parameter 1 or 4; decision), collaboration model (traditional against Info-Smooth; decision), Demand Forecast (moving average over 1 or 5 periods), Lead Time (1 or 5 periods, fixed), Inventory Safety Stock (factor fixed at 1), backlog of unfilled orders, unlimited production, storage and transport capacity; performance: Bullwhip ratio (order variance ratio at each echelon), net stock variance ratio

Title: A priori assessment of a smart-navigated unmanned aerial vehicle disaster cargo fleet
Venue: Simulation: Transactions of the Society for Modeling and Simulation International (SIMULATION)
Specific aspect / SC aspect: Analysis and optimization: fleet size, cargo capacity, speed and range of a UAV disaster cargo fleet, and the rule assigning UAVs to requests (humanitarian distance against geographic distance), judged by loss of life probability and completed requests
Optimization/prediction method used: Greedy near-optimal assignment of UAVs to requests by minimum humanitarian distance, run inside the simulation; fleet specifications compared as scenarios, and the assignment rule compared with and without the humanitarian distance by a t-test
Comments: A MATLAB object-oriented model of a UAV fleet that delivers two types of relief cargo from a hospital base to 13 request zones in a rural Puerto Rico region after a hurricane. Requests arrive at random and expire after about 1 or 3 hours. UAVs are assigned to requests by a humanitarian distance that grows with urgency. Varying fleet size, cargo capacity, speed and range, the runs measure the share of requests that expire (loss of life probability) and the requests completed per UAV. A fleet of three UAVs is judged the best size for this region, and the humanitarian distance cuts expired requests compared with using geographic distance alone.
Any attributes: base (one hospital), request zones (13, one drop-off point each), UAV fleet (size, standard 3), UAV cargo capacity (units, standard 2), UAV speed (40 km/h), UAV range (35 km), delivery and refill delay (5 minutes), request types (cargo type X or Y), request arrival (probability per minute; about 3 X and 9 Y per hour), request expiration time (normal, mean 1 hour for X and 3 hours for Y), request priority (exponential in time to expiry), UAV-to-request assignment rule (humanitarian distance, k = 1; decision), simulated horizon (12 hours); performance: loss of life probability (share of requests that expire), requests completed, requests completed per UAV, expired requests per hour

Title: Minimizing the bullwhip effect in a supply chain: a simulation approach using the beer game
Venue: Simulation: Transactions of the Society for Modeling and Simulation International (SIMULATION)
Specific aspect / SC aspect: Optimization: order quantity and reorder point of an EOQ-based fixed-order policy with a no-backlog rule and goods in transit counted, for the four-echelon beer game, to minimize total chain cost and the bullwhip effect
Optimization/prediction method used: Full-factorial scenario search in two steps (order quantity at a reorder point of 30, then reorder point at Q = 12), with the cost of each scenario compared by simulation
Comments: An Arena discrete-event model of the four-echelon beer game (factory, distributor, wholesaler, retailer) with the original game's lead times, costs and demand step. Each node orders a fixed quantity when its stock falls below a reorder point less goods in transit, and only if the upstream node can fill the order. Two rounds of experiments (order quantity, then reorder point) find the cheapest setting, an order size of 12 and a reorder point of at least 90. The chain cost is about half that of a published system dynamics solution of the same game.
Any attributes: four nodes (factory, distributor, wholesaler, retailer), end-customer demand (5 units for 5 weeks, then 9), delivery Lead Time (2 weeks), factory production time (2 weeks), order lead time (1 week), initial inventory (12 per node), inventory holding cost (0.5 per unit per week), backlog cost (1 per unit per week), order quantity Q (fixed size; decision), Reorder level (decision), no-backlog ordering rule (order only if upstream stock covers Q), goods in transit counted in ordering, inventory visibility across nodes (VMI), run length (52 weeks); performance: total chain cost, holding and backlog cost per echelon, stock level over time

Title: Improving operational efficiency of iron ore logistics by rail using simulation

Comments: A Planimate discrete-event model of the rail transport of iron ore from a mine to a steel plant in Iran, across seven stations (loading, support, internal unloading and four intermediate ones). Title: A colored petri net-based modeling method for supply chain inventory management
Venue: Simulation: Transactions of the Society for Modeling and Simulation International (SIMULATION)
Specific aspect / SC aspect: Analysis: effect of information sharing, demand forecasting and demand variance, and of canceled orders and deliveries, on order variance amplification and stockout amplification in a four-echelon serial chain modeled with Colored Petri Nets
Optimization/prediction method used: Simulation-based scenario comparison of four configurations (traditional or information sharing, with or without disruptions)
Comments: A hierarchical timed Colored Petri Net model, built in CPN Tools, of a four-echelon serial chain (retailer, wholesaler, distributor, factory) with an external supplier and an end customer, using an (R, S) order-up-to policy. Bullwhip results are compared with published ones to validate the method, and a state space analysis checks for deadlocks and liveness. Runs then compare traditional and information-sharing chains, with and without moving-average forecasting, at two demand variances, and with orders or deliveries canceled by one echelon for 12 periods. Stockouts are amplified upstream when forecasts are updated, more so with information sharing, and cancellations by an echelon propagate stockouts downstream.

Title: Hybrid modeling of collaborative freight transportation planning using agent-based simulation, auction-based mechanisms, and optimization
Venue: Simulation: Transactions of the Society for Modeling and Simulation International (SIMULATION)
Specific aspect / SC aspect: Analysis and optimization: auction-based allocation of containers to trucks in a shared urban freight network, with the number and capacity of trucks set by simulation-optimization, judged by truck distance per container, container lead time and truckload utilization
Optimization/prediction method used: OptQuest simulation optimization (scatter search and tabu search with neural-network screening), a CPLEX winner-determination program for each auction, and weighted multi-objective runs to trace Pareto fronts
Comments: An AnyLogic agent-based model of a Physical Internet freight network in Louisville, Kentucky. Containers from 26 e-commerce warehouses and 5 gateways travel through 13 hubs on trucks, and an auction decides which carrier takes each container, using an optimization program (CPLEX). OptQuest then searches for the truck count and capacity that minimize distance per container, lead time, or maximize truckload use, alone or combined as a Pareto trade-off. The collaborative auction gives distance and lead time within about 3% of closest-truck and earliest-truck baselines, with higher truck utilization (about 77%).
Any attributes: 26 warehouses, 5 gateways, 13 hubs, 1 airport, container arrival rates (1.8 per hour at warehouses, 18 per hour at gateways), trucks (number 25 to 50, capacity 5 to 10 containers; decisions), truck speed (50 km/h), maximum wait time (2 hours), dock time (5 minutes), load time (5 minutes), sort time (15 minutes), fixed cost (US$3 per container), variable cost (US$1 per km-container), profit margin (15%), carrier selection by auction (bid from cost and fill rate; decision), shortest-path routing between hubs, time windows; performance: average truck distance per container, average container lead time, truckload utilization, combined weighted objectives

Title: Modeling and simulation for inventory management of repairable items in maintenance systems
Venue: Simulation: Transactions of the Society for Modeling and Simulation International (SIMULATION)
Specific aspect / SC aspect: Analysis: effect of three reordering policies (reorder point with order quantity, min-max, lot-for-lot) with backordering, and of lead time, repair time, repair probability, unit costs and number of repair stations, on the inventories of new, repaired and faulty repairable items, backorders, unavailability and cost
Optimization/prediction method used: None. One-factor-at-a-time parametric analysis of the simulation (Tables 5 to 13)
Comments: An Arena discrete-event model of a maintenance system in a manufacturing plant. Production lines send corrective and preventive faulty items of three types to a repair shop, and the model holds three inventories (new, repaired, faulty awaiting repair) and orders new items with a triangular lead time. It compares three reordering policies with backordering, and a one-factor-at-a-time analysis varies lead time, repair time, repair probability, costs and repair stations. Lot-for-lot gives the highest unavailability and backorders, and reorder point with order quantity gives the lowest.
Any attributes: three item types with corrective (Poisson) and preventive (scheduled) arrivals, probability of repair (10 to 80%), repair time (uniform, 1 to 6 days), Lead Time (triangular 5, 7, 10 working days), reorder point and order quantity (EOQ; decisions), minimum and maximum inventory levels (decisions), periodic review period (10 days), ordering cost (5,000 MU per order), holding cost (100 MU per item per year), repair stations (one technician, two shifts), initial new stock (twice the lead-time demand), backordering, discard of unrepairable items; performance: on-hand inventory of new, repaired and in-repair items, holding time, backordered items, unavailability (downtime), ordering cost, holding cost

Title: Dynamics inventory decisions in perishable supply chain considering sudden change in demand and risk attitude
Venue: Simulation: Transactions of the Society for Modeling and Simulation International (SIMULATION)
Specific aspect / SC aspect: Analysis and optimization: effect of the retailer's inventory adjustment coefficient and risk attitude on system stability and on retailer loss from spoilage and fresh-product shortage, under a sudden demand change in a two-stage perishable supply chain
Optimization/prediction method used: Grid search over the inventory adjustment coefficient and the risk coefficient (19,521 strategy pairs), with the Lyapunov exponent of the simulated order series used to find the stable region
Comments: A system dynamics model of a two-stage fresh food supply chain with a supplier that produces to order and a retailer that orders by the VIOBPCS rule with exponential smoothing of demand. The retailer's risk attitude, taken from prospect theory, changes how spoilage losses enter the order. Fresh stock turns into discounted stock after one week and is spoiled after two. A short demand step is applied, and a program sweeps the inventory adjustment coefficient and the risk coefficient to find the stable region (Lyapunov exponent) and the lowest retailer loss over 100 periods. Moderate risk aversion with a moderate adjustment coefficient gives the lowest loss.
Any attributes: two nodes (supplier, retailer), potential demand (200 with a step of 500 between periods 20 and 30), split of demand into fresh (80%) and discount (20%), Shelf Life (one week fresh, then discount, then spoilage), production delay and transport delay (Lead Time; values not stated), exponential smoothing forecast, inventory adjustment coefficient (0 to 4; decision), retailer risk attitude (-6 to 6; decision), pull production (make to order), no returns, non-negative orders; performance: Lyapunov exponent, quantity of spoilage, shortage of fresh product, retailer loss

Title: Simulation of cloud-based blood supply chain: a system dynamics approach
Venue: Simulation: Transactions of the Society for Modeling and Simulation International (SIMULATION)
Specific aspect / SC aspect: Analysis: how donation, processing and hospital factors shape wastage, fill rate and inventory level in a blood supply chain, and comparison of a cloud-based real-time information-sharing policy with the conventional chain
Optimization/prediction method used: None. A one-at-a-time sensitivity analysis (all parameters changed by 20%) and t-tests of the cloud-based policy against the conventional chain
Comments: A Vensim system dynamics model of the blood supply chain of Iran with three subsystems: donation and collection, processing and production, and hospitals. It tracks whole blood, red cells, platelets and plasma with expiry. The model is checked with structural tests and compared with historical series, and a sensitivity analysis changes every parameter by 20%. A cloud-based policy is then added in which real-time inventory information guides donation, blood bank ordering and hospital ordering. Against the conventional chain, it lowers the wastage rate and raises the fill rate.
Any attributes: donor classes (first-time, lapsed, regular) and donation rates, fixed and mobile collection centers (capacitated), blood banks and hospitals with stocks of whole blood, red cells, platelets and plasma, separation percentage (98%), Shelf Life and expiry, Lead Time (zero to blood banks, one day to hospitals), first-in-first-out issuing, no returns, hospital reorder point and maximum stock coverage (monthly review), blood bank stock coverage, emergency orders, cloud-network adoption by donors (decision); performance: wastage rate, fill rate, inventory level

Supply chain problem: Resilience Modeling, Risk Estimation and Mitigation
Title: Simulating Maritime Chokepoint Disruption in the Global Food Supply
Specific aspect / SC aspect: Analysis: effect of a 30-day closure of the Panama Canal, the Suez Canal or the Strait of Gibraltar, in each month of 2017, on the monthly wheat, maize and soybean imports of four importing countries and on ship arrivals at the Strait of Malacca
Optimization/prediction method used: None. Simulation-based scenario comparison, with differences from the no-closure baseline tested at the 0.05 level
Comments: A Simio model of dry-bulk shipping of wheat, maize and soybeans from six exporting countries (nine ports) to four importing countries, driven by UN monthly export data, in which ships take the shortest route and reroute when a chokepoint closes. Each of three chokepoints is closed for 30 days in each month of 2017 and compared with a baseline over 30 replications. Closures cut the imports of several importers sharply (soybeans to Spain by up to 97% under a Gibraltar closure), and Panama or Gibraltar closures raise ship arrivals at the Strait of Malacca by 20% to over 90%.
Any attributes: exporting countries (6) with export ports (9) and importing countries (4) with import ports, Product(s) (wheat, maize, soybeans), monthly export quantity per exporter and commodity (triangular within 10% of UN monthly exports, seasonal), ships with Maximum Load Capacity (55,000 dwt), travel speed (triangular within 10% of 14 mph), Link distance (waypoints on a satellite map), shortest-route selection with dynamic rerouting at closure and reopening, chokepoint closure (Panama Canal, Suez Canal, Strait of Gibraltar) with Disruption Duration (30 days) and disruption month; performance: monthly imports per importer and commodity, percentage change of imports from the baseline, ship arrivals at the Strait of Malacca

Title: Dynamic Pricing as a Mitigation Strategy against Supply Network Disruptions with Price-Sensitive Demand – an Agent-Based Model
Specific aspect / SC aspect: Analysis and optimization: disruption costs of a four-tier supply network when both producers are disrupted for 1 to 20 days, under fixed prices and under dynamic cost-plus prices whose smoothing window (price elasticity) is searched for each level of customer price expectation
Optimization/prediction method used: Uniform space-filling design over the price smoothing parameter (30 to 200) and the mean customer price expectation ($60 to $150); the best smoothing value per setting is taken from the simulation results
Comments: An agent-based model of a four-tier network with three suppliers, two producers, two wholesalers and three retailers, each replenishing by an order-up-to policy with daily review and setting its price daily as a moving average of its costs plus a margin. Customers buy only below a normally distributed maximum price and wait a limited time. Both producers stop for 1 to 20 days after the network reaches balance. With fixed prices the network cost rises sharply once buffer and in-transit stock are used up; dynamic prices cut the total disruption cost but shift the loss to the downstream entities, and longer disruptions call for less elastic prices.
Any attributes: suppliers, producers, wholesalers, retailers (four tiers), raw material price at the source ($9 to $12) with a delivery time, Production Capacity (20,000 pieces), Production Lead Time (uniform, Table 1), Production Cost (setup and variable), Order Cost (fixed, and variable at the upstream price), Inventory Replenishment Policy (order-up-to, daily review), Inventory Order-up-to Level (target inventory per entity), Lead Time (delivery time 2 to 6 days), Transportation cost ($0.5 per piece), Inventory Holding Cost(s) (18% of value per year), Backorder Penalty (20% of the current price per day, upstream entities), Backorders or Lost Sales (lost sales at retailers valued as opportunity cost, customers wait up to five days), Selling Price (cost-plus with a moving-average smoothing window, decision 30 to 200), customer maximum price (normal, mean $60 to $150), Demand (normal, mean 250 and standard deviation 10 per retailer per day), Demand Forecast or Forecast Error (retailer forecast in its price calculation), Node Disruption (both producers on day 1500), Disruption Duration (1 to 20 days); performance: Disruption Cost (total network and per entity), saved disruption costs relative to fixed prices

Title: A Simheuristic Algorithm for the Location Routing Problem with Facility Sizing Decisions and Stochastic Demands
Specific aspect / SC aspect: Analysis and optimization: the number, location and size of depots, the allocation of customers, the vehicle routes and the safety stock that minimize the expected total cost of a location routing problem with stochastic demands, and the cost and reliability effect of choosing depot sizes from a set instead of a fixed size
Optimization/prediction method used: Simheuristic: biased-randomized constructive heuristic for depot maps and sizes, then iterated local search with Monte Carlo runs (100 short, 5,000 intensive) estimating expected cost and reliability; safety stock set by a fast simulation over 0% to 10%; results of the fixed-size simheuristic of Quintero-Araujo et al. (2020) and the best deterministic solution as references
Comments: A location routing problem with random customer demands in which each opened depot takes one of five sizes, so depot sizing becomes a decision beside location, allocation and routing. A simheuristic builds depot maps and routes with biased randomization and an iterated local search, and Monte Carlo runs estimate the expected opening, routing and route-failure costs and the reliability of the plans. On 12 adapted benchmark instances at three demand variance levels, flexible sizes lower the expected total cost in 11 of 12 instances (up to 6.7%) against fixed sizes, mostly through lower opening cost, and the stochastic plans are more reliable than the best deterministic plans.
Any attributes: candidate depots (5) with Location, five alternative sizes per depot (0.5 to 1.5 times the instance size, r = 0.25) and Establishment Cost (fixed cost plus a size-dependent variable cost), number, location and size of depots to open (decisions), customers (30 or 40) with Location and Demand (log-normal, mean from the instance), Demand Variability (variance 0.05, 0.10 or 0.20 times the mean), customer-to-depot allocation (decision), vehicle routes (decision), shared homogeneous vehicles with Maximum Load Capacity, Transportation cost (routing cost), safety stock as a share of vehicle capacity (decision, 0% to 10%), corrective action after a route failure (reactive round trip or preventive detour, the cheaper one); performance: Supply chain cost (expected total cost of opening, routing and route failures), opening cost, routing cost, stochastic cost, solution reliability

Title: Investigating Brexit Implications on the Irish Agri-Food Exports: A Simulation-Based Scenario Mapping Model
Specific aspect / SC aspect: Analysis: effect of post-Brexit customs and SPS checks at ports, of moving Irish cheese flows from the UK Landbridge to direct ferry routes to the continent, and of missing check infrastructure at west GB ports on truck transport time and remaining shelf life of cheese traded between Ireland, Great Britain and the EU
Optimization/prediction method used: Simulation-based scenario comparison
Comments: An AnyLogic model of roll-on/roll-off freight between Ireland, Great Britain and the EU over 16 maritime routes, with products, trucks, vessels and ports as agents and the check procedures as discrete event flows. Trucks carrying cheese leave suppliers, pass port checks, sail on scheduled vessels with set capacities and reach distributors. Strict checks raise transport times many times over and cut remaining shelf life by up to about a quarter, direct routes to Cherbourg, Rotterdam and Zeebrugge keep times and shelf life acceptable, and closing west GB ports creates a bottleneck on the Dublin-Liverpool route.
Any attributes: suppliers, distributors and ports (Ireland, GB, EU), maritime routes (16), Transportation Type (accompanied and unaccompanied trucks, Ro/Ro vessels), vessel departure frequency and Maximum Load Capacity, product volumes converted to trucks by average unit weight, customs and SPS check routing shares (green, orange, red) and check times, route choice (Landbridge or direct routes, decision), port closure (west GB ports, Node Disruption), Shelf Life (cheese); performance: Travel Distance or Time (transport time by flow), remaining shelf life

Title: Equitable Allocation of Scarce Resources during the COVID-19 Pandemic: A Case Study for Convalescent Plasma Distribution
Specific aspect / SC aspect: Analysis: comparison of a population pro-rata weekly allocation of scarce convalescent plasma from the central blood supplier to five regional hub sites with two adjusted rules that move units toward sites with high unmet demand or high recent case counts
Optimization/prediction method used: Simulation-based scenario comparison of three allocation rules (pro-rata, AdjShip, AdjShipCC)
Comments: A stochastic simulation of the weekly distribution of COVID-19 convalescent plasma by the provincial blood supplier to one hub site in each of five British Columbia health authorities over the 22 weeks of a clinical trial. Plasma supply and the arrivals of infected patients, who are hospitalized, recruited and randomized to plasma, are calibrated to provincial case counts, with two plasma groups and unmet demand lost each week. Pro-rata allocation by population understocks the sites that use the most plasma and overstocks the others. The two adjusted rules lower total unmet demand and even out the ratio of received units to units used across sites, and the gain grows as supply gets scarcer.
Any attributes: central blood supplier distribution site and five hub sites, one per health authority, with spoke hospitals aggregated (Type), convalescent plasma units in two plasma groups, A-O (p = 0.81) and B-AB (Inventory Product(s)), weekly supply calibrated from case counts with donation and antibody probabilities, weekly shipment from the supplier to each hub (Inventory Reorder Period), no transfer between hubs, patient arrivals as a non-homogeneous Poisson process by day of week calibrated to case counts (Demand), hospitalization probability and delay (uniform 5 to 12 days), recruitment and randomization probabilities (2:1 plasma to standard care), blood group compatibility, unmet demand not carried over (Backorders or Lost Sales), allocation rule: pro-rata by population share, AdjShip with a threshold on the proportion of unmet demand and an inventory threshold equal to the average past demand, AdjShipCC by recent case counts (decision), sparse and extremely sparse supply (scenarios); performance: demand (Demand Placed), unmet demand (Shortage), proportion of unmet demand, ratio of total received inventory to total utilization

Supply chain problem: Inventory Analysis and Optimization; Resilience Modeling, Risk Estimation and Mitigation
Application domain: Agriculture and Food; Humanitarian and Emergency
Title: Optimisation of the national grain reserve system using a two-phase algorithm
Specific aspect / SC aspect: Optimization: amount of each grain type that each Chinese province holds in reserve and the province where it is stored (off-site storage), minimizing the expected annual holding, transport, shortage penalty and replenishment cost under natural disaster and grain price surge events
Optimization/prediction method used: Two-phase simulation optimization: an immune algorithm with simulated annealing searches the reserve schemes on few replications, then OCBA allocates further replications to select the best of 40 candidates; compared with a linear programming scheme from earlier work and with random search plus OCBA
Comments: A stochastic simulation of the local grain reserves of the 31 provinces of mainland China, in which a province may store part of its unprocessed grain in other provinces. Disaster and price surge events generate daily demand in a province, an expert estimate with error decides whether remote stock is shipped back in order of distance with a lead time, unmet demand is penalized and stocks are restored after the event. Each reserve scheme is costed by repeated simulation inside a two-phase search. The best scheme found stores about 40% of grain remotely and lowers the annual cost by about 16% against the current all-local scheme, mainly through holding cost, and sensitivity runs show the minimum local reserve ratio binds while warehouse capacity does not.
Any attributes: provinces as reserve nodes (31), Inventory Product(s) (rice, wheat, corn, soybean unprocessed; mixed processed grain), reserve amount by grain type, owner province and storage province (decision), Inventory Capacity (warehouse capacity per province), minimum local reserve ratio by grain safety group (0.3 to 0.5), target reserve level (3, 4.5 or 6 months of consumption), processed grain reserve (3 to 7 days of consumption), Inventory Replenishment Policy ((s, S) for local unprocessed grain), Inventory Reorder Level (s = 0.2S), Node Disruption (natural disaster events, Poisson once per year; price surge events with a probability per province), Disruption Duration (uniform 3 to 10 days and 10 to 60 days), Demand (daily demand per province, normal), demand estimation error (coefficient of variation 0.1), share of demand served by local reserves (80% disasters, 60% price surges), consumption order of grain types, shipment order by increasing distance, Lead Time (preparation and shipping between provinces), Link distance, Transportation cost (fixed 100,000 RMB per shipment and variable rate by distance), Inventory Holding Cost(s) (per province), Backorder Penalty (twice the procurement price), procurement price and salvage value (replenishment cost); performance: Supply chain cost (expected annual total cost), Inventory carry cost, Transportation cost, Backorder or Shortage Cost, replenishment cost, domestic reserve percentage, national grain weighted distance

Title: Enhancement of Vendor-Managed Inventory Planning Through Deep Reinforcement Learning
Specific aspect / SC aspect: Optimization: daily replenishment quantities for vendor-managed inventory (VMI) of semiconductor products, set by a TD3 agent trained per product and jointly over 100 product-customer combinations, with a shipment penalty that trades the number of shipments against keeping the stock within the agreed minimum and maximum levels
Optimization/prediction method used: Deep reinforcement learning (TD3 with a continuous action space, single-product and multi-scenario training); hyperparameters tuned by Bayesian optimization (Tree-Structured Parzen Estimator); benchmarks: the company's current policy and the DQN results of Ahmad et al. (2022)
Comments: A semiconductor supplier replenishes VMI stock held at its customers, who pull from it daily and share weekly forecasts, under a 28-day order lead time. The VMI system is written as a Markov decision process whose daily step updates the stock with the recorded customer pulls, and a TD3 agent learns the number of packages to ship, with a penalty on each shipment. Tested on three products and on 100 product-customer combinations of the company, the agent keeps the stock inside the minimum-maximum band on more days than the current policy, and a larger shipment penalty brings the number of shipments down toward the current level at some loss in that share.
Any attributes: VMI stock position at the customer, minimum and maximum stock levels (customer-agreed, forecast-based), Lead Time (order lead time 28 days), Demand (daily customer pulls, recorded), Demand Forecast or Forecast Error (weekly customer forecasts, forecast bias), packing size, maximum number of shipments per day, initial inventory (zero), replenishment quantity in packages (decision), shipment penalty (varied 0 to 2); performance: percentage of days with no violation of the minimum-maximum band, Customer Service Level (alpha service level, days without stock-out), Demand Fulfilled (beta service level, share of demand met from stock), Total Shipments

Supply chain problem: Logistics Optimization and Route Planning; Resilience Modeling, Risk Estimation and Mitigation
Title: Imparting Adaptiveness and Resilience to Parcel Delivery Networks: A Digital Twin Centric Simulation Based Approach
Specific aspect / SC aspect: Analysis: effect of a festive-season surge in parcel volume on a large parcel delivery network around one major hub, and comparison of interventions (an added sort schedule, more sorting capacity, diverted paths, more loaders, more vehicles, removal of the hub) on on-time delivery, transit time, dwell time and utilization
Optimization/prediction method used: Simulation-based scenario comparison (what-if levers)
Comments: A composite digital twin of a parcel delivery company built from agents for the parcel feeder, facilities (collection centers, hubs and destination centers with sorting machines, chutes and loaders) and fleets that move parcels along trails of paths between facilities. The model is set to a subset of a real company's network of 857 facilities and about 90,000 parcels a day and run for 30 days. A surge of 5 to 10 times on selected trails through the main hub lowers on-time delivery from almost 100% to about 76% and raises dwell time sharply. Adding a sort schedule, raising sorting capacity or diverting parcels to underutilized facilities restores on-time delivery, and the hub can be retired with its flows moved to a nearby facility.
Any attributes: parcels and shipments with weight, size, shape, destination and service type (Product(s)), parcel mix by size class, trail volume and daily parcel inflow of about 90,000 (Demand), surge of 5 to 10 times on selected trails (demand disruption), facility types: collection center, hub, destination center (Type), inbound and outbound doors, chute capacity, sorting machine capacity, sort schedules with timing and throughput (Production Capacity), loaders and sorters (Resources), paths between facilities with mode: road, rail, air, water (Transportation Type), trails as sequences of paths that route parcels (decision), fleets and fleet count (Fleet Composition), hub removal and redirection of flows to another facility (network structure decision), rerouting of 90% of the surge volume to underutilized facilities (decision); performance: maximum hub capacity utilization (Resource Utilization), on-time delivery rate, average parcel transit time, package throughput utilization (Throughput), average dwell time (Waiting/Turnaround Time)

Title: Combining simulation and reinforcement learning to reduce food waste in food retail
Venue: Simulation: Transactions of the Society for Modeling and Simulation International (SIMULATION)
Specific aspect / SC aspect: Optimization: order quantities of three perishable products at a food store, set by reinforcement learning agents trained on a discrete-event simulator, against a past-week ordering baseline and a dynamic reorder-level baseline, to cut food waste and raise profit
Optimization/prediction method used: RL (PPO in discrete and continuous form, SAC, DQN; Stable Baselines3) with two reward functions, compared with a past-week order baseline and a dynamic reorder-level baseline; SLSQP inside the demand synthesis
Comments: A day-by-day discrete-event simulator of food retail with wholesalers, stores and customer groups, in which deliveries, expiry, orders, price setting and purchases are events. The case has one wholesaler with a two-day delivery time, one store that may order on Mondays and Thursdays, and one customer group whose daily demand for strawberries, potatoes and carrots is synthesized from yearly and monthly statistics. RL agents set the order quantities, and over 1000 runs of a three-year test period they cut food waste sharply against a baseline that orders last week's sales, while DQN also earned more profit than the reorder-level baseline from the literature.
Any attributes: wholesaler, store and customer group (population 10,000), products (strawberries, potatoes, carrots), Shelf Life (normal, means 8, 28 and 75 days), Lead Time (2 days), ordering allowed on Mondays and Thursdays (Inventory Reorder Period), Order Quantity or Lot Size (agent decision, ten discrete levels up to about two weeks of peak demand), Inventory Reorder Level and Inventory Safety Stock (baseline: dynamic reorder level with safety stock of one week of expected demand), Purchasing Cost (historical weekly wholesale price), Selling Price (historical weekly retail price, set on Mondays), Demand (daily demand synthesized from yearly and monthly statistics with noise, seasonality and weekday foot traffic), Demand Forecast or Forecast Error (forecast within 20% of actual demand), uniform customer choice among items in stock; performance: Inventory Waste (share and value of food wasted), Net profit

Supply chain problem: Resilience Modeling, Risk Estimation and Mitigation; Logistics Optimization and Route Planning
Title: Clustering-based resilience in urban quick-commerce last-mile delivery: a simulation study under hub capacity disruptions
Specific aspect / SC aspect: Analysis: how the customer-to-hub assignment produced by 15 clustering methods, together with flexible or rigid reassignment, keeps on-time delivery and fill rate stable when micro-fulfilment hubs lose part or all of their capacity
Tools used to build the model: Python 3.9 (NumPy, pandas, OSMnx, NetworkX, scikit-learn, scikit-fuzzy)
Optimization/prediction method used: Simulation-based scenario comparison. Fifteen clustering methods (centroid, medoid, density, soft, graph, probabilistic and greedy families, for example K-means, K-medoids, DBSCAN, Fuzzy C-Means, spectral clustering, Gaussian mixtures) form the hub zones; shortest-path routing with NetworkX; elasticity and coefficient-of-variation analysis of the outputs
Comments: A multi-day simulation of quick-commerce last-mile delivery on the OpenStreetMap road network of a dense district of Kolkata, with synthetic customers whose daily orders follow a Poisson process and are served by capacitated micro-fulfilment hubs. Fifteen clustering methods set the hub zones and the customer-to-hub assignment, and hubs lose 25 to 100% of their capacity under six disruption scenarios, with unserved customers either moved to the nearest hub with spare capacity or lost. Disruption severity drives most of the change in fill rate and on-time delivery, and soft and medoid-based clustering (Fuzzy C-Means, K-Medoids) keep both metrics the most stable. Flexible reassignment raises the fill rate under severe disruption but lowers on-time delivery.
Any attributes: customers with daily demand from a Poisson process (Demand), customer and hub coordinates (Location), micro-fulfilment hubs with nominal capacity including a buffer that is drawn down by the assigned demand each day (Inventory Capacity), inventory buffer of 0 to 50% above assigned demand (Inventory Safety Stock), road-network distance between customer and hub (Link distance), average vehicle speed (10 to 40 km/h), OTD threshold (delivery time limit), hub zoning and customer-to-hub assignment by clustering method (decision), reassignment policy (flexible to nearest hub with spare capacity, or rigid) (decision), Node Disruption (graded hub capacity loss of 25, 50, 75 and 100% on a target subset of hubs, six scenarios), unserved demand lost (Backorders or Lost Sales), demand growth up to 20% per year; performance: fill rate, on-time delivery (OTD) rate, coefficient of variation of fill rate and OTD across disruption scenarios
